speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head O of the Estimates be reduced by $100." Sir, I would like to declare my interests, both as a medical doctor practising in a restructured hospital, as well as the Advisor to a facility providing day care for seniors and people with disabilities.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is a well-known aphorism that a chain is only as strong as its weakest link and, by the same token, a healthcare system is only as strong as its least amenable portions.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In fact, many of the concerns that were raised in a White Paper drafted by the Government Parliamentary Committee for Health some years ago and, indeed, raised by many Members of this House, both past and present, have been addressed, to varying degrees, by these bold initiatives.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But it may surprise many that most of these measures benefit the outliers rather than the majority, as those who are manifestly sick represent the tip of the disease iceberg, the apex of the healthcare pyramid.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A truly comprehensive and robust healthcare system must look beyond treating the sick and look beyond medical treatment alone.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, we have to focus on preventing disease and reducing the disease burden.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have previously remarked that the key to a healthy society is that, in the long run, it depends less on how well you treat sick people, but more on how you keep people from falling sick.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Managing the healthy is probably one of the biggest challenges facing healthcare workers.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How does one go about convincing people to continue making the right lifestyle choices, day after day, over one's lifetime?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The lure of just that one more cigarette, that extra helping of char kway teow, that one extra can of soda, that extra piece of cake, is often just too difficult to resist.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Similarly, making the decision to eat more fruits and vegetables, to exercise more, always seems just that one day away.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is certainly not something which Singapore would like to be on the leader board!

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The WHO has also reported that, globally, there is a frightening rise in the incidence of diabetes.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Last year, during the Budget Debate, I remarked that much can be done to nudge Singaporeans to take greater ownership of their health.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Anti-tobacco measures should be stepped up even further and, while some may argue that unhealthy behaviours should be penalised, by the same token, healthy choices can be incentivised.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I will speak later on how we can encourage healthy eating through fiscal levers.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Foods that are available in schools, for instance, could be more closely regulated to help stem the menace of childhood obesity.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can the Ministry provide an update on the Healthy Living Masterplan?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What is being done for young Singaporeans to cultivate healthy living habits?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am a strong believer in the one-patient-one-family doctor concept, as the formation of a strong patient-doctor bond provides a singularly effective and efficient way to good health for life.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Ministry has enunciated this principle in years past and I would like to hear from the Ministry what progress has been made on this front.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I also appreciate the various health screening programmes that have been implemented over the years, with many at little or no cost to the individual.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For instance, community health screening activities are held regularly in my constituency of Queenstown, as they are all over Singapore, but concerns have been raised on how we can ensure that screen-positive patients do follow up on their follow-ups.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Has the Ministry been looking at ways in which the transition from community health screening to follow-up in clinics can be made more seamless and accessible?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, a strong healthcare system also needs to look after those who have undergone treatment but continue to have residual incapacity.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In a rapidly ageing society like ours, we need to bolster measures to ensure that our seniors remain healthy and active and are able to age gracefully and to do so in the community where they have lived most of their lives.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Medical care in Singapore is among the best in the world but, often, even with the best and most dedicated treatments, patients are left with residual disabilities.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What is broken can sometimes not be made whole and the sick cannot always be made well again.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would also like to ask the Ministry if they are looking at new models of assisted living in the community, apart from the more traditional avenues like nursing homes and day care centres.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The reason I ask this is both from personal experience and also from interactions with my residents and patients.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is, sometimes, a difficult choice to make.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some loved ones may need extra help in their daily activities, but to consign them to a nursing home may take away too much of their liberty and many scientific and medical articles have shown that such restriction of liberties may actually do more harm for the individual than good.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would also like to ask how we can better support community caregivers.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Last year, it was announced that we were working on a home and community care plan, to facilitate ageing-in-place.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How does the Ministry intend to ensure that our seniors receive holistic and seamless care?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Are there plans to utilise technology for care delivery?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If this is not feasible, can Page: 127 we assist patients with disabilities, seniors and their caregivers with transport arrangements or subsidies from their homes to the various healthcare institutions?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A significant number live alone, or with a partner or spouse who is dependent on them.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In Queenstown, for example, we have several initiatives to meet this challenge.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have a home monitoring trial; we have a community guardian network; we also have things like a charitable free funeral service for those who pass on alone without kin.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can I ask if the Ministry has plans to manage this demographic challenge?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My final concern lies in a slightly sensitive topic, but one which we should discuss as a community.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is a wake-up call that we should pay greater attention to improving end-of-life care.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What plans does the Ministry have to improve palliative services and end-of-life care for Singaporeans?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Just as this year's Budget has been expansionary in the service of economic transformation, our healthcare policies have likewise been inclusive and expansionary over the past decade to meet changing and increasing healthcare demands.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But even as we increase national spending on healthcare, we should be mindful that the spending should be prudent and sustainable and that the relationship between healthcare spending and health outcomes is not always linear, as many countries have found to their detriment.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am concerned about the strain on the public purse and whether future generations can sustain such spending.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, in business where the target is surpassed by a wide margin, sometimes, it is due to good performance; sometimes, it is due to good fortune; and sometimes, it is due to the target being set too low.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I urge MOH to review this performance indicator.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One hundred minutes or 1 hour and 40 minutes is not an acceptable time for our patients to wait, especially the elderly.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I suggest that we change this Page: 128 time to 45 minutes to provide a more meaningful KPI for good performance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MOH publishes the median and 95th percentile waiting times for polyclinics.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This points to what is probably the huge difference in waiting time between those who make appointments and those who walk-in.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I suggest that waiting times be published separately for those who had made appointments and those who walked-in.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am aware that Internet phone and mobile apps are available for making polyclinic appointments.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, in SMU's recent customer satisfaction survey, satisfaction with polyclinic waiting times fell in 2015.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is there more we can do to cut waiting times for those elderly Singaporeans who tend to walk-in?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe this is done at some polyclinics but not all.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: I asked about this during the COS debate three years ago and was assured by the Minister that MOH adopts a multi-pronged approach to address the queue at our SOCs.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: During this long wait, a patient's condition could deteriorate and he could develop complications which will be harder and more expensive to treat.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister share, from the time an appointment is made to the consultation with the specialist, what are the average range, median and 95th percentile waiting times for consultation at SOCs for subsidised patients?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: After the consultation, what are the average range, median and 95th percentile waiting times for the conduct of investigations and tests like MRI or CT scans and for elective surgery?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: How do these numbers compare with three years ago?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Moving forward, to help benchmark SOCs' performance, will MOH publish SOCs' appointment waiting times regularly on its website for the median and 95th percentile, like it does for waiting times for admission to wards and registration and consultation at polyclinics?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The long waiting times seem to affect subsidised patients much more than unsubsidised patients.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first is by being referred to a medical social worker who will do a financial assessment for the patient.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second is for patients to get a referral letter from the doctor at the hospital which they are instructed to take to the polyclinic.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This letter will provide that the polyclinic should refer the patient back to the hospital.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first method may not be suitable for patients who do not need a financial assessment from a medical social worker to justify a downgrade.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For the second method, the patient needs to see the doctor at an SOC first to get a referral letter to the polyclinic.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The patient then sees another doctor at the polyclinic.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the polyclinic, such patients have to wait in the same line as other patients, who are genuinely sick, to see the doctor.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The polyclinic doctor then directs patients to the referral counter for a letter referring them back to the same hospital.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The polyclinic doctor may charge the consultation even though the patient did not actually require a medical examination for the referral.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does the polyclinic doctor really have to do any medical consultations since he will know from the specialist's referral letter the purpose for the visit?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: From my description of the typical scenario, it would seem that much time is wasted on the part of the patients by way of waiting and transport and on the part of the polyclinic doctors having to attend to what seems essentially an administrative task.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The whole process becomes unnecessarily inefficient and bureaucratic.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It also involves unnecessary expenses on the part of the patients.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One would have thought that their request to transfer from private to public care can be dealt with adequately by an administrative staff at the hospital.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At most, perhaps the patient only needs the attention of the doctor at the SOC who can even handle this outside his clinic hours as an administrative task done without requiring the presence of the patient.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The doctor can always ask to see the patient if he has some questions for the patient.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have described the details of the process to try and highlight inefficiency and the endless bureaucratic process.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The process could be done in a hospital itself.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This would help to relieve some of the workload on the polyclinics and the medical social workers and reduce unnecessary waiting and travelling times for patients.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It will also reduce queues at hospitals as well as the polyclinics.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It will be a win-win situation for patients, doctors, hospitals and polyclinics.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Minister Gan Kim Yong, would you want to report on progress?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Ministry of Health (MOH) has stated that overseas Singaporeans should contribute to the national risk pool as "part of collective responsibility".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Ministry says this will also enable them to benefit from MediShield Life protection anytime they choose to return to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This stand makes sense for those overseas Singaporeans who know that they expect to return to Singapore to live.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, there are Singaporeans who have made their home in other countries for decades.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These include Singaporeans married to foreigners and raising children overseas, sometimes because the foreign spouses are not able to find suitable work in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: They enjoy high standards of healthcare in these countries, which they pay taxes for.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Others have emigrated as families and now have access to healthcare at prices more affordable to them.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Some chose to live abroad because they could only obtain adequate coverage for their serious health conditions there.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These Singaporeans are better covered overseas and will probably never tap on MediShield Life.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is there a compelling case that no opt-out should be allowed at all?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: MediShield Life means coverage for all, including the most vulnerable among us.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, when MediShield Life was introduced, it was expected to account for a bigger chunk of Integrated Shield payouts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, this prospect was quickly put to rest with the announcement by the various insurers that any rise in the top-up portion of premiums would only be frozen for 12 months.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Ministry consider informing the insurer that the moratorium should also include a freeze on riders as well, since this would have been a backdoor to work around the moratorium, insofar as keeping healthcare costs affordable as a whole?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How does the Government work with the insurers to check on any unjustified rise in premiums and to what extent can the Government intervene, if and when premiums are unjustifiably raised?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In view of this new environment of data analytics, will the Ministry release more data in conjunction with the insurance companies so that the public will be in a better position to track and appreciate the rising trend of claims and specifically identify areas of over-consumption?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What does the Ministry do to ensure that private hospitals and doctors do not take maximum advantage of private insurance plans?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Does the Ministry consider this to be a growing problem and how does it plan to mitigate it?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Prior to launch, the plan was framed as an affordable Integrated Plan providing greater choice to consumers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, will the Ministry consider increasing the MediSave withdrawal limit amount for Singaporeans of all ages, especially older Singaporeans who choose this plan, so that they can be paid for completely through their MediSave account?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Preventive medicine is a topic I am passionate about and I have been advocating this preventive healthcare.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In the year 2000, I was privileged to spearhead the two-year islandwide "Check Your Health" programme to screen those above 50 years of age for diabetes, hypertension and high blood cholesterol.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Although we are in a better situation now with more people readily going for regular health screening, we must continue to push for the detection and treatment of these three chronic diseases, and especially so for diabetes.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Diabetes is a killer disease that slowly steals life away.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: It can slowly destroy body organs, resulting in blindness, lower-limb gangrene, kidney failure, stroke, cardiac disease and so on.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: If we can promote better control of diabetes, we will see less of these complications that cause pain and burden upon sufferers and their family members.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Patient non-compliance is not only limited to the failure to take medications, but also the failure to make lifestyle changes, undergo tests or keep appointments with physicians.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Non-compliance can be due to factors that are patient-centred, therapy-related or healthcare system-associated.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The patient-centred factors can be demographic, such as age, gender, educational level and marital status, and psychological, such as patients' beliefs and motivation towards the therapy, negative attitudes, patient-prescriber relationship, patients' understanding of health issues and general knowledge.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The therapy-related factors include the route of medication, duration of treatment, complexity of treatment and the side effects of the medicines.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The healthcare system-related factors include availability or accessibility of care and the physician.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Could MOH address these non-compliance factors and mitigate them in order to have better success with diabetes?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Would MOH also incentivise people to stay healthy with token rewards?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our home palliative care services do good work for Singaporean patients from all walks of life.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have seen it myself when I visit residents and attend funeral wakes in Clementi.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: They tell me about how their loved ones were helped at home during terminal illness.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have seen how they looked after my own cancer patients that I see in a professional capacity.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And I also saw how they brought comfort to my father, during his last days, as a cancer patient, terminally ill.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: These nurses and doctors make the greatest difference because of the human touch.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: A human touch for patients at home, patients from all walks of life.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Home visits, listening to patients and their families, giving advice and guidance to caregivers.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And they can teach us as well, at the systems level, how to look after other patients at home – the chronic sick, the frail, the very elderly – because travelling to a clinic takes time.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It can be challenging for some patients and their families if the patient is bed-bound after a stroke or if your loved one cannot sit up for long because of pain.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For many seniors, age becomes almost irrelevant when they are physically, mentally and socially healthy, and they will have the freedom to do as many things as the young can do.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a firm believer in preventive health, I would like to know how the Ministry can encourage and enable medical follow-ups of seniors found to have at-risk conditions.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have always found it challenging to encourage our seniors to go for their follow-up treatments and therapies.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some are worried that they would discover more serious medical conditions and would prefer not to know.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And yet others claim they have no time.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Whatever medical conditions they have, if treated early, it can prevent deterioration, escalating healthcare costs and poor quality of life.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: An idea I would like to propose is to tap on the community network of seniors, where elderly neighbours and friends can encourage their peers to see their doctors for follow-ups.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Seniors want to age in familiar environments surrounded by people they know and who understand and care for them.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They also need easy access to care centres and doctors.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Their caregivers also need support from the community in caring for their senior family members.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What are the major initiatives for aged care services?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The Action Plan, "A Nation for All Ages", is targeted at the individual level, the community level, as well as the city level.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Can I ask about MOH's action plan for community level health promotion for our seniors and what community networks they can tap on, bearing in mind that we also want to align with those that are existing in the constituencies?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: As we know, we cannot disengage an individual from his/her community and, in fact, the latter has a value-added effect and positive impact on well-being, mental wellness and happiness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Having a trusted group of friends and "kakis", the seniors can be made to feel differently and a lot better.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Will we see a more well integrated range of services and networks, readily available to our seniors at no or low cost, up close and personal, near their residences?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Can we make these stimulating, broad ranging and exciting as well for our seniors in their active ageing years?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: As we also plan to integrate the seniors with their multigeneration families and extended families, can the Ministry also consider family-friendly activities and networks which will be appealing to all ages, in order to target multi-generational involvement?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: One of the initiatives that has been announced include co-locating eldercare and childcare facilities in new Housing and Development Board (HDB) developments to maximise opportunities for interaction among the different generations.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: The programme will include healthy lifestyle campaigns, community activities and interventions for mature workers at workplaces.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: I welcome these initiatives for I have encountered many elderly who may not know how to select nutritious food and do the appropriate physical activities to keep fit.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Would the Ministry consider providing general guidelines, taking into account age bands, that show the recommended types of physical activities that a senior can do if he has certain medical conditions?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Teaching them, their family members and community volunteers to recognise signs of illnesses, including dementia, is also important as early detection and intervention will contribute to more effective treatment.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Would the Ministry share further details of the National Seniors' Health Programme to promote good health in seniors?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: What kind of interventions will be introduced at their workplaces?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: How does the Ministry plan to encourage more seniors to participate in such programmes and activities?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: One critical aspect that we must not neglect is the health of our seniors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Without health, our seniors cannot be active and lead a meaningful life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I am heartened by the slew of pro-elderly measures introduced over the past years.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These are needed to enable a graceful and meaningful retirement for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But to achieve a truly caring society, we cannot rely only on the Government or a few charitable organisations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It also ensures that the human touch will not be lost as we work towards more efficient eldercare and as we embrace greater use of technology.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I believe this is a very meaningful way of engaging seniors who are fit and keen to do something constructive in their retirement.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Moreover, seniors can also relate to seniors better, as they may share common challenges and language.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some of the PGAs in my constituency are Pioneers themselves and they take great pride in their work as ambassadors.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Life expectancy in Singapore is among the highest in the world and our Health Adjusted Life Expectancy, which measures years lived with "full health", is among the top three globally.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In short, Singaporeans can expect to live longer and healthier.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: There are encouraging signs that more Singaporeans are choosing a healthier lifestyle.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Today, more than a quarter of Singaporeans consume at least one serving of wholegrain products per day, more than three times the rate in 2004.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: There are some worrying trends which I will elaborate later.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But, first, let me give an update on our Healthcare 2020 Master Plan.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Over the last five years, MOH has expanded our capacity in all sectors.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The three hospitals will continue their ramp-up this year and are expected to bring online another 270 beds.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang asked about wait times for our Specialist Outpatient Clinics (SOCs).

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: From 2013 to 2015, SOC attendances increased by 5%, largely due to the increase in subsidised attendances by our seniors, which grew by 26%.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: These patients would have benefited from higher subsidies, especially for the Pioneer Generation (PG).

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: During the same period, private SOC attendances actually fell by 5.3%.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For private patients, median wait times stayed about the same at eight days, while the 95th percentile wait times also increased, from 47 to 58 days.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Nevertheless, we have made improvements in the 50th percentile and 95th percentile wait times for specialties, such as Rheumatology and Immunology, Gastroenterology, Ophthalmology and Neurology, despite increasing attendances at these SOCs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At Alexandra Hospital, for example, the overall median wait time is less than a week and, at the 95th percentile, 12 days.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, patients who need an earlier appointment can ask their doctor to refer them to hospitals with a shorter wait time.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For patients with more serious and time-sensitive conditions, our hospitals and polyclinics have protocols in place to arrange for faster appointments at our SOCs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For example, the median wait time for new subsidised appointments for urgent cardiac conditions and suspected cancers was around one week.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In fact, for cardiology and cardiothoracic surgery, the median wait time has improved from 14 days to six days.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have been managing the wait times for our SOCs in three ways.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: First, we optimise the SOC appointment system to give priority to urgent cases.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We also reduce "no-shows" by reminding our patients of their appointments via messages.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Second, we are working with polyclinics and general practitioners (GPs) to ensure that only patients who need a specialist's care are referred to our SOCs and, for patients who have recovered and are well, to help them transition back to primary care.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Third, we have added new SOC capacity through developments, such as the Nnational University Hospital (NUH) Medical Centre, National Heart Centre and Ng Teng Fong General Hospital.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang cited the case of a patient experiencing a long wait for an appointment and biopsy results.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, I would be happy to look into the circumstances of the specific case if Mr Low can provide the details.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Mr Low also asked about the time taken for computed tomography (CT) scans.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For the first quarter of 2016, the median wait time for a routine subsidised outpatient CT scan was between one and three weeks for most hospitals and has remained stable over the past three years.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I should explain that the timing of the CT scans may also be a result of scheduling to coincide with the reviews by doctors.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For conditions that require urgent scans, hospitals are able to fast-track these cases, whether in the wards, in the SOCs or at the accident and emergency (A&E), on the same day or the following day.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Other than hospital capacity, we have also added about 1,200 nursing home beds and 60% more home-care, day care and home palliative care places between 2011 and 2015.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Looking forward to 2020, we are on track to add more than 6,600 places in community care, home-care and palliative care, as well as 7,900 beds in acute hospitals, community hospitals and nursing homes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Mr Leon Perera asked about wait times at our polyclinics.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Polyclinic attendances have been growing over the years, from 4.5 million attendances in 2011 to 4.9 million in 2015.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Mr Perera is correct that wait times for patients with appointments is, indeed, lower than wait times for walk-in patients.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Over the past few years, polyclinics have been encouraging more patients to use the appointment system.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Currently, all patients with chronic conditions, many of whom are elderly, are offered appointments for their next chronic visit.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In 2015, 70% of these chronic patients visited the polyclinics by appointments.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will continue to help more patients use the appointment system.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In the meantime, we are adding capacity and improving processes to meet the primary care needs of our population.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The last four years, we redeveloped the Geylang and Tampines Polyclinics and have just completed an expansion of Marine Parade Polyclinic.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Lower and middle income patients and all PG patients now have an alternative as they can tap on the PG package and the Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS) to enjoy subsidised primary care at private GP clinics instead.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have also made significant moves in addressing Singaporeans' concerns over affordability.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In 2014, we launched the PG Package which provided 450,000 Singaporeans with more help with their healthcare costs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For lower- to middle-income Singaporeans, we have raised the subsidies for outpatient drugs and specialist care.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: With CHAS, I spoke about this just now, about 1.4 million Singaporeans, including Pioneers, are able to benefit from Government subsidies at participating GPs and dentists close to their homes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Since 2012, we have more than doubled the number of participating clinics to 1,500.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have introduced more flexibility in the use of MediSave to help Singaporeans with their healthcare costs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Today, Singaporeans can also use up to $400 per MediSave account per year to pay for their outpatient chronic disease management.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Last November, we introduced MediShield Life to provide better protection for all, for life.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: To date, many Singaporeans have benefited from MediShield Life.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Take, for example Mdm Sung, a Pioneer living in Ang Mo Kio.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Late last November, Mdm Sung had a stroke and her family brought her to Tan Tock Seng Hospital where she was warded for 11 days.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: She continued her rehabilitation and recovery for eight days at the Ang Mo Kio Thye Hwa Kwan Community Hospital near her home.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The total bill for the stay came up to $16,900 and, after subsidies, Mdm Sung needed to pay $6,400.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Before MediShield Life, Mdm Sung, who was uninsured, would have had to pay the full $6,400, but with MediShield Life coverage, she only had to pay about $3,300, close to half the original bill.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And all of this was paid through her MediSave.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Today, Mdm Sung is back to living with her son and his family.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: She has four children, 10 grandchildren and six great grandchildren – a great example for our population strategy.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: A few weeks ago, the whole family came together to celebrate her 85th birthday.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We wish Mdm Sung and her family the best of health.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: MediShield Life, together with Government subsidies, MediSave and MediFund, will continue to help many Singaporeans like Mdm Sung and low-wage workers mentioned by Nominated Member Thanaletchimi in her Budget speech earlier, giving them greater peace of mind that their medical treatment will be affordable.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked about the coverage for overseas Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: MediShield Life was introduced to give all Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents assurance of universal healthcare coverage, regardless of their health condition, situation and background.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: MOH is aware that Singaporeans based overseas are concerned that MediShield Life coverage is mandatory.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We recognise that the overseas Singaporean community is diverse and individual circumstances vary considerably.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The MediShield Life Council will conduct targeted engagements with overseas Singaporeans as part of their MediShield Life coverage review, while bearing in mind the principle of universal coverage.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The effort to pilot Community Networks for Seniors announced by the Minister for Finance earlier, is a whole-of-Government approach to "close the last mile" in supporting successful ageing for seniors in our community.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As highlighted by Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef and Ms Tin Pei Ling, this pilot is not about introducing another new service for seniors in the community, but an effort to strengthen partnership and coordination among key stakeholders, such as agencies and community organisations, so that we can work together, as a team, to better meet the needs of our seniors and build a stronger community for our seniors to age in place.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have studied the system in other countries.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Many developed countries with ageing populations are facing similar challenges as us.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: One important lesson we can learn from them is that doing more of the same cannot be the solution.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We need a paradigm shift in our approach to ageing and health.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It will take time, but we must start now.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We must make good use of the next few years to plan ahead and design a system that meets our growing needs in a cost-effective and sustainable manner beyond 2020.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We can do so, with three paradigm shifts: first, to move beyond the hospital to the community; second, to move beyond quality to value; and third, to move beyond healthcare to health.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will make it easier for patients to access appropriate care, help them recover faster and enhance health outcomes while keeping costs affordable and sustainable.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: To do this, we need to reshape our health delivery system.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The first aspect in reshaping our system is to link up care through the Regional Health System (RHS).

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will need to further strengthen the integration of RHS.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: An example of this is to develop structured care pathways to better care for patients across settings.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The Eastern Health Alliance RHS has introduced an integrated care pathway for patients with hip fracture, across providers.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Patients who have sustained hip fractures are quickly identified and put on the hip fracture pathway.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is crucial, as starting the rehabilitation process early leads to better mobility outcomes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Upon discharge, patients attend day rehabilitation near their homes, as needed, to optimise their functional outcomes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Such pathways require various partners in the RHS, and sometimes among RHSes, to work closely to deliver seamless care to patients, for better outcomes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Our vision of "One Singaporean, One Family Doctor" remains relevant.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We want to transform primary care to be the first and continuous line of care so that Singaporeans can access good quality care in the community.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As Dr Chia Shi-Lu pointed out, the key is to build a trusted relationship between GPs and Singaporeans, so that your family doctor has a deeper understanding of you and your family's health needs and can, therefore, provide better guidance and more appropriate treatment when needed.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Minister of State Lam Pin Min will elaborate on how we are strengthening the primary care sector later on.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As we reshape our health delivery system and move beyond the hospital to the community, we need to make similar shifts in how we develop and deploy our healthcare workforce.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Our healthcare workforce must be future-ready, so that healthcare professionals can continue to enjoy fulfilling careers and can readily acquire new skills and capabilities.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Senior Minister of State Amy Khor will talk about how we are creating good healthcare jobs for Singaporeans and fostering industry-relevant skills through the national SkillsFuture framework.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: MOH, together with our public healthcare institutions, will be looking into job redesign and the use of technology to not just simplify the work for our healthcare teams, but to also work in a different way to deliver care to our patients.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Minister of State Chee Hong Tat will share how productivity and innovation can support our healthcare workers and improve patient care.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu said we must care for Singaporeans from birth to death, and I agree.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The issue of death is a sensitive one, especially in our "pantang" Asian society.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: These are difficult conversations which we must have, not just among family members, but also at the national level, that is, if we want our loved ones and family members to have dignity, comfort and peace of mind as they walk through their last journey.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This requires a whole-of-society approach and we are encouraged to see organisations, such as the Lien Foundation, raise these topics at the national level.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Through the Agency for Integrated Care (AIC), we have also been working with our hospitals and community partners to raise the awareness of Advance Care Planning (ACP).

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: ACP allows individuals and their families to better understand their preferences towards the end of life and to fulfil their wishes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Take, for example, the late Mr Phang who was admitted to Dover Park Hospice after being diagnosed with terminal cancer.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Through ACP, the hospice staff were able to establish that his preference was to pass on at home, so that he was able to spend his last days in a familiar environment, together with his wife.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This was a great source of comfort to his wife.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: She was grateful to the hospice staff for establishing his end-of-life wishes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Minister of State Chee Hong Tat will be elaborating on further enhancements we are making in palliative care.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As we transform our healthcare system, we have to be mindful of the long-term implications on sustainability.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The current challenging economic outlook is a timely reminder of the need to ensure sustainability, not just for ourselves but for future generations.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Therefore, we need to choose care that is appropriate to needs, so that we can make the best use of our limited resources.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It is for this reason that we have a co-payment feature throughout our healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For example, MediShield Life has co-payment features like claim limits, deductibles and co-insurance to help guard against over-consumption or over-provision of services.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: However, many Singaporeans have private Integrated Shield Plans that are "as charged", which means they have no claim limits, and some buy extra riders to cover the deductibles and co-insurance.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Such features could lead to a "buffet syndrome" since all the cost will be paid for by third parties, by someone else.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This contributes to rising healthcare costs for everyone and eventually pushes up premiums.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will need to study this carefully to ensure sustainability.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Emerging healthcare technologies are becoming increasingly expensive and we need to ensure that the outcomes derived from these technologies are commensurate with the costs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This will help patients, care-givers and physicians to make more informed decisions on treatment and avoid over-provision of services that will eventually drive up costs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As we move beyond hospitals to the community and beyond quality to value, we also have to move beyond delivering healthcare and focus on providing good health to nurture a healthy nation and a healthy people.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: To do this, we need to arrest the causes of ill health early and reduce the progression of long-term chronic diseases.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: While the Health Adjusted Life Expectancy has improved over the years, as I mentioned earlier, Singaporeans are also living with ill health longer – one-and-a-half years longer than in 1990.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have observed several worrying trends in recent years.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Decreasing activity across all age groups and the increasing consumption of excessive calories and fat leading to a rising obesity rate.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Obesity is the major risk factor for chronic diseases, such as Type 2 diabetes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As noted by Dr Lily Neo and Dr Chia Shi-Lu, diabetes is, indeed, fast becoming a major global healthcare concern.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: When I sat in my seat, I looked to my left and I looked to my right.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: On my left is Mr Lim Swee Say and on my right is Ms Grace Fu.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I asked him yesterday, "Do you have diabetes?" He proudly declared, "No".

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I was too polite to ask her, but she does not look like she has diabetes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The bad news is: one in three means I have the highest risk of getting diabetes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But the good news is: we can change.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We do not have to accept it and we can reduce the risk.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Of those who have diabetes, one in three Singaporeans has not been diagnosed.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And among those diagnosed, one in three has poor control of their condition.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The following images on-screen may be graphic but they are examples of what some Singaporeans endure daily.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Left undetected, untreated or poorly managed, diabetes can lead to heart disease, stroke, kidney failure, blindness and amputations.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In fact, four Singaporeans a day lose a limb or appendage due to diabetic-related complications.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: These complications reduce the quality of life for the patient and increase the burden on the individual, families and society as a whole.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: However, the long-term cost of diabetes, taking into account the psycho-social burden, is far more than this.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We want to help Singaporeans live lives free from diabetes, and for those with the disease, to help them control their condition to prevent deterioration.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will engage stakeholders and develop detailed action plans together, but let me outline our broad strategy.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: First, we will work on upstream prevention to promote a healthy lifestyle and reduce obesity rates in order to cut down on new diabetes cases.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Broadly, we are doing this by ramping up our health promotion efforts through a twin food-and-exercise strategy.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will improve the dietary quality in schools, communities and workplaces, and learn from successful international regulatory strategies.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: To encourage more people to exercise, we will expand ongoing programmes, such as the National Steps Challenge and Sundays@The Park, as well as introduce new programmes and bring them to schools, workplaces and our community.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The risk of developing diabetes is 30% to 40% higher among active smokers than non-smokers, and we will be doing more to curb smoking rates as part of this plan.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Minister of State Lam Pin Min will be leading our efforts in developing the NurtureSG Plan to tackle many of the preventable risk factors for our youths.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will be working closely with the Ministry of Education (MOE) to develop and implement this plan.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Second, we will strengthen early screening and intervention to identify the disease early, especially those at risk.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Screening plays an important role in our war by picking up cases earlier, starting interventions and, thus, reducing the likelihood of the gory images I showed you previously.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We hope that earlier intervention and basic lifestyle changes can even reverse the pre-diabetes state and get such individuals back to health.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, you are never too old to make lifestyle changes and take back your health.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Third, we will support better disease control to slow disease progression and reduce complications.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For those with diabetes, we need to do our best to help them have a good quality of life, at all stages, by having good control over their disease.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This can help to reduce or delay complications and give patients better quality of life.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: (In Mandarin):   This year, we are going to declare war on diabetes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Many of my colleagues asked me, "Why so serious?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Why do you want to say, 'declare war'?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Why so aggressive?" Diabetes is a problem that is getting more serious by the day.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The possibility of them contracting diabetes as they grow older also increases.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And it is not just them who suffer.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Therefore, we have no choice but to mobilise the entire population to declare war on diabetes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We should also, each of us, play a part by eating responsibly and exercising and ensuring our own health.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At the same time, we also need to do intervention earlier and do screening much earlier.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Together, we can also seek help if we need to.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Together, nationwide, we can have a healthier lifestyle.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: (In English): The key to winning the war on diabetes is for all Singaporeans to be engaged in the battle.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The key partners in this war are the individuals, his family and the community.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: By working together, we hope to create an environment that makes healthy choices easy, but Singaporeans also need to play their part by eating healthily, exercising often and going for the recommended screenings and follow-ups.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We can also play a part in encouraging and helping others to do so.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will be increasing public awareness about diabetes and empowering individuals to take control of their health.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The war on diabetes will not be a quick battle, but a long war requiring sustained efforts.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Results of our efforts can only be seen in the long term, but we must persevere.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And if we succeed in shifting mindsets and changing habits, we will be able to curb not just diabetes but other related chronic diseases, such as heart disease, as well.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And we will improve the lives of Singaporeans and reduce the burden on their families.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: All Singaporeans need to play an active role in their health journey and in the war on diabetes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We all need to make sensible lifestyle choices and informed decisions in our health.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The Government will do its part to provide a supportive environment, but we cannot do this alone.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: If we are able to do this together, we will achieve better health, better care and a better life for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Mental health is very much an integral part of general health.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: They tend to be more prevalent in lower-income households and they usually cannot cope with employment and cannot fit well in society.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Those that suffer from substance abuse also have violent tendencies.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: As the majority of Singaporeans live in densely populated HDB estates, we must be cognisant of the harm that mental patients can bring not only to themselves and their family members but also to neighbours and people in the community.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: There are many types of mental disorders; from mild ones like anxiety, personality disorder and depression, to moderate ones like kleptomania or compulsive stealing, compulsive gambling and substance abuse, to other severe psychotic diseases.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: In general, mild cases have good prognosis if treated early.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Many such mental patients also need other social assistance and thus SSOs can facilitate that simultaneously.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: I know that there is a Community Mental Health Team set up by the Institute of Mental Health (IMH) to provide psycho-social rehabilitation for people suffering from mental disorders in the community.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: However, the purpose of the team is to facilitate patients to be discharged from and not to be re-admitted to IMH.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: I am concerned in this respect, as there are already too many undiagnosed and untreated mental cases in the community.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Will it be better for IMH to discharge such patients to community hospitals or psychiatric nursing homes instead?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: I really hope IMH is not so psyched up to prematurely discharge patients without considering the overall implications.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Non-compliance has been a problem, especially for mental patients, to the detriment of the patients themselves and the community.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: And I would say that Singapore has made progress in mental healthcare over the years; I have seen it.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: There is greater awareness, better intervention and more support.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: I would also say that few, if any, in our society would dispute the importance of ensuring mental wellness.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: However, there is still much that we can do.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: One critical obstacle to effective mental healthcare is the stigma faced by sufferers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Stigma may be perpetuated by the lack of understanding and media portrayal, but also, by real day-to-day problems that are left unsolved.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: I have raised examples about this in my speech last year, so I will not touch on it again this year.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Together, these threaten to deepen the prejudices that people have of those suffering from mental health issues.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Meanwhile, efforts to strengthen community mental healthcare must not stop, so that those who need care will continue to get the care they need.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Hence, I would also like to ask: one, whether there is any update on the Community Mental Health Masterplan; two, how are patients who have "graduated" from IMH reintegrated back into the community and workplace; and third, and lastly, some communities have implemented networks involving voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs), Government agencies and grassroots leaders.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: MacPherson, for instance, has a Community Mental Health Programme supported by AIC, IMH and the South East Community Development Council since 2012.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: At the very least, amongst the volunteers and staff who have to frequently face residents, there is greater awareness of the signs and symptoms which aid early detection, greater appreciation of the challenges people with mental health issues face and greater sensitivity in how to engage them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: I am wondering if there are plans to roll this out more extensively to more communities.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It is also time for us to put more focus on mental health.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Mental illness, while perhaps less understood, is no less real than physical illness.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: There is also the stigma and lack of understanding which patients and their loved ones combat daily.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Currently, our MediSave, MediShield and MediFund (or 3Ms) framework allows support for mental illnesses, but it is limited.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Compare this with a daily limit of $450 for other patients who have been hospitalised.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Mental illness is as real and debilitating as other illnesses.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Funding from the 3Ms and other insurance plans should be on par with coverage for other conditions.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Companies, too, need to be encouraged to provide equal levels of support and coverage for employees who suffer from mental health issues.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This may not always be classified as a mental or even physical illness, but the strain on our healthcare costs and infrastructure can be massive.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister give an update on what has been done in the last few years to ensure our care systems are able to deal with the future increase in the number of dementia sufferers and whether there are plans to expand pilot projects, such as "dementia-friendly" town?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: As there is stigma, many are not coming forward to be diagnosed early enough or for follow-up regular treatments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Thus, it is important to have services and counselling in the community, in a less threatening environment, compared to being in an institution or a ward.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: At Geylang Serai, I have got Silver Ribbon sited at my community club (CC) at My Wellness Centre and they do house visits and counselling at the CC as well as the residents' homes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Therefore, we need to have more such programmes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: What we do at Geylang Serai is we create awareness of mental health problems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: We give talks, organise mental wellness seminars, hold World Mental Health Day celebrations annually, launch suitable books and educational materials, mental health road shows and we even have a Geylang Serai Mental Wellness Taskforce operating for the last several years, comprising 10 partners from the relevant industry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Therefore, we hope that this model can be initiated and replicated elsewhere as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: This is under the initiative of WeCare@geylang Serai.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: In fact, this year, we are actively involved in organising and partnering other agencies in The Asia Pacific Mental Health conference in October.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: My grassroots leaders (GRLs) will be sharing programmes, experiences and initiatives and we need such initiatives in the community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: What are MOH's plans to strengthen community mental health support network and framework at the national level?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Will we be seeing a new blueprint as well?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: As we face the silver tsunami, the number of seniors who suffer from dementia is expected to rise.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: One in 10 people aged 60 and above, and half of those aged 85 and above have dementia.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: What preventive measures can we introduce to the public so as to reduce or temper the expected surge in dementia cases?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: (In Mandarin):   As we face the silver tsunami, the number of seniors who suffer from dementia is expected to rise.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: What preventive lifestyle changes can Singaporeans be encouraged to adopt to reduce the risk of getting dementia?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: An MOH study shows that the risk of dementia is 25 times higher for housewives and retirees than the working people.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Working and participating in community activities actively may help to slow down brain degeneration.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Hence, we should encourage and help more housewives and retirees to stay active and healthy.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: (In English): Would the Ministry share with us the latest initiatives for the early detection and treatment of dementia?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Also, what is the Ministry's long-term plan to support persons with dementia who are living in the community?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Research has shown that allowing them to age-in-place would be less costly to society.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Those who care for dementia sufferers are three times more distressed than other caregivers.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Many have to stop work, which may put them in financial situation.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: What kinds of support schemes are there to help and relieve family caregivers?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Will MOH consider allowing standard health screening, including dementia screening, to be done at private GPs at subsidised rates?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Not all will need institutional care; many will still want to live in the community.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: We must find ways to help our senior Singaporeans with dementia, such as helping them to lead as normal a life as possible, reducing their risk of getting lost or confused during their daily activities, and ensuring they do not become socially isolated because ongoing mental stimulation is healthy for the ageing brain.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: These issues will affect all our housing estates, especially mature estates, with many Pioneers, many senior citizens.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Can MOH tell us what the Ministry is doing to support Singaporeans with dementia who are living in the community, as well as their caregivers and loved ones?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, some reports suggest that the current supply of nurses providing home-based care may not be sufficient to meet the expected increase in demand.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Several providers of home nursing care are employing foreign nurses on foreign domestic Work Permits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This could compromise the quality and development of home-based care in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Furthermore, the 10,000 patients only refer to those needing palliative care.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These nurses can be provided with the right training to become professional community nurses attached to hospitals to provide home-based care.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second, will the Ministry consider developing a comprehensive Hospital and Home Programme modelled on the programme in Australia?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under the Hospital and Home Programme, hospitals will provide inpatient treatment for acute care patients whose conditions allow them to receive treatment in their own homes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is not limited to seniors or the terminally ill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The community nurses could then act as key care providers, conducting medical check-ups and providing portable medical services to the home-based patients.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The community nurses could also make use of telehealth technology to engage in non-site consultations with hospital-based doctors in the homes of the patients.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: I am repeating my call in this House again to make this service available quickly in order to lessen the need for high-cost stay in the tertiary institutions, especially the acute hospitals.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: With our ageing population, homecare, where many discharged patients can be looked after in their homes, will be an increasing demand and an important part of our healthcare structure.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Whilst I agree that homecare will incur many medical personnel to visit patients in their own homes, MOH should relook the usage of healthcare workers and consider using not only full-time paid personnel but also family members, community volunteers and so on.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Such healthcare workers can be trained in a matter of weeks.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: In England, it takes only three weeks of intensive training to equip them with the necessary skills.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: A team of staff and nurses look after the elderly weak and partially disabled seniors with medical conditions in their homes.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: They assist them with their daily and medical needs in three HDB rental blocks.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Perhaps MOH can duplicate such a homecare model in other constituencies, too.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: For specific problems, specific services will be required, for example, day care rehabilitation, physiotherapy, speech therapy, nursing care and even for mental diseases and dementia as well as mood management services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: How is MOH planning to ramp up some of these services, which means not just the infrastructure but also the needed manpower and trained personnel?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: For those with significant physical disability and mental health issues, their families need to make arrangements for their care, as the former would have to go out to work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: With the call for a later retirement age and also more active employment for our seniors and women, therefore, more day care facilities will be required in the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: With these centres, we will also have to ensure that care standards are met and the ratio of patient-to-caregiver is acceptable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Here is where I would like to suggest that perhaps we seek and tap on the retired nursing pool as well as train active retirees so that they can help to contribute a few hours a day at least to this required pool.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: This can be very tiring for them as well as for their caregivers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: It is important that they have access to integrated and holistic care so that they will not end up shuttling from one place to another.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: What are the Ministry's plans to enable senior-centric care to take place?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: An example of an ideal situation would be like this.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: A senior goes to an SAC daily to take part in activities, socialise and exercise.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: The staff at the centre are familiar with his general health conditions and problems, and assist him to take his medications.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: When the elderly exhibits certain health symptoms, they are able to take note and alert his family members or, if he lives alone, to refer him to the appropriate agencies.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: When he goes for his medical appointments, the tests and treatments are preferably arranged on the same trip to minimise travelling.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: In addition, when he needs to move around different departments within the hospital, there will be volunteer guides to help him, especially for an elderly who can only communicate in his vernacular language.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: When he grows more frail and has to stay at home, he or his family will be able to get assistance from day/night nurses or part-time care-givers at affordable rates.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: What kind of support or resources can we provide their families and caregivers, especially if they have long-term patients, to take care of challenges like dementia or depression?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: What is the Ministry's plan in meeting this demand?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: What are the constraints or challenges anticipated, if any?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Also, are there lessons that we can draw from countries more experienced in caring for the aged?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: For instance, Japan is the world's fastest ageing society and it was said that the "epidemic of dementia" had already arrived.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Given that it had to address this challenge much earlier, what can we learn from Japan about the needs of our old, especially those with dementia, and what can we do to address these needs?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: With an ageing population, demand for palliative care will be expanding.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Many terminally ill patients prefer to be at home with their family members and staying in their familiar surroundings in their final days.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: They feel more comfortable compared to being hospitalised.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: But for hospice care at home, cost is always an issue, besides other factors.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Many families are apprehensive about how to cope with their terminally ill family members even though they want to fulfil the final wishes of their loved ones.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Thus, they may be more prepared to do so, if they can get more support on hospice care at home.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Could MOH expand palliative care with more personnel and facilities?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: These terminally ill patients need home visits by palliative care doctors to control symptoms, such as pain.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: They need social workers to support the psycho-social needs of patients and their family members as well as recognising and facilitating the final wishes of the patients.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Many patients and their family members also need counselling.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Presently, not many doctors and nurses are interested in palliative care.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Increasing numbers of terminally ill patients will also impose an increasing demand on palliative care in-patient beds and services.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Hence, we need an expansion in these facilities as well.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Palliative care can be costly and it may be a strain for many patients.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: The additional factors of increases in healthcare material costs and remuneration for healthcare workers will also drive up the costs of hospice and palliative care.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: And how many have written in to appeal for subsidies for the high costs of inpatient charges at the hospices?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: A thorough review of the ElderShield scheme is long overdue and it is perhaps the right time for the Ministry to not only include hospice and palliative care under the scheme, but to also review the adequacy of the subsidies and payout period of the ElderShield scheme.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin, you have two cuts, please take them together.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I declare my interest as an educator in empathy awareness.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Benchmarked against 80 countries, we are sixth in the affordability of care, eighth in the quality of care, and our weakest score was in community engagement at 22nd.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, a 2014 survey by Lien Foundation showed that two in three Singaporeans still do not even understand what palliative care is.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This lack of public awareness and hospice referral is partly because our doctors and nurses struggle with handling death.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I can testify to what it is like to encounter such a statistic in real life.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: A junior doctor that attended to my father in a hospital here exhibited zero empathy in the way he broke the news to us that my dad had terminal cancer.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This highly educated, articulate young man told us, "Here is the result, it is not good.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Even when we broke down in front of him, he was completely blank and indifferent, and that is very disturbing to me.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Thankfully, the rest of the doctors I encountered on the journey were much more sensitive.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: My dad passed away in a hospice and it was a very gentle place for him to die, thanks to the staff there.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, I am deeply grateful to every Singaporean who is involved in palliative care.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is an incredible gift to the dying, as well as the living.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: My experience made me wish that more families here could experience the mercy of a good death.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, I have just two simple requests: one, keep up the good work of making palliative care even more accessible and affordable; two, make socio-emotional awareness a core component of training for all healthcare professionals.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
