text: Our family doctor can be our partner in helping us stay healthy and in providing us with good and affordable care close to us.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Many Singaporeans see a doctor when we come down with an illness, such as a bad cold.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: With a regular family doctor, such visits can develop into a strong doctor-patient relationship over time.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As our family doctor develops a holistic understanding of our family's medical profile and health needs, they will become our health advocate in identifying risk factors and can offer more targeted, timely and individualised advice and plans to manage our health.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For those with chronic diseases, we can manage our condition better by having a family doctor who understands our condition well and supports us with quality management and treatment.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Our family doctor must also have some understanding of our family, social and work situation to advise us on making lifestyle changes and adhering to treatment.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: They can also refer us appropriately if we require more specialised medical attention and help coordinate our care with other providers.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Tan Heok Lim has been seeing his family doctor, Dr Leong Choon Kit, for the past 14 years.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: He feels comfortable with Dr Leong's care and has continued seeing him for his medical needs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This enables Dr Leong to care for Mr Tan holistically – from health screening to diagnosis and management of chronic conditions, such as hypertension.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: With deeper understanding of the family, Dr Leong has recommended suitable health screening for Mr Tan's wife, who has a strong family history of diabetes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mrs Tan was found to be borderline diabetic and Dr Leong was able to intervene early through advice on lifestyle modifications, to prevent the progression of diabetes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Currently, Dr Leong manages the chronic conditions of Mr Tan, his wife and his son.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: And I am happy to hear that both Mr Tan and his son have also successfully quit smoking, with encouragement from their family members and Dr Leong.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We want to call on Singaporeans, especially those with chronic conditions, to take the first step in identifying and sticking with a regular family doctor.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To facilitate this, we will review our policies to help strengthen doctor-patient relationships in primary care.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As we progress on the journey to realise our vision of "One Singaporean, One Family Doctor", we will continue to engage our GP and polyclinic colleagues to co-create the future primary care landscape, in particular, to achieve better chronic disease management in the community.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We are mindful to ensure sufficient primary care capacity with the ageing of the population and a growing chronic disease burden.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Our polyclinics will continue to play a key role, especially in the management of complex chronic diseases.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In recent years, we have announced the development of new polyclinics and redevelopment of existing ones.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Since 2012, we have also strengthened partnerships with private GPs to provide subsidised care to Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We have also developed new models of primary care, such as the Family Medicine Clinics or FMCs, since 2013.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The FMCs are multi-doctor practices, with onsite nurses and other allied health professionals, delivering comprehensive team-based care, especially for chronic disease management.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As part of our continual efforts to better serve our residents, we have been redeveloping existing polyclinics.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The new polyclinic is expected to be operational by 2020 and will be designed to cater for future primary care needs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will continue to review and evaluate FMC development as part of our efforts to strengthen and improve primary care.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: With these range of developments, we have tried to support the growing needs in primary care.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To address Dr Tan Wu Meng's concerns, residents in the West can look forward to three new facilities – the new polyclinics in Jurong West and Bukit Panjang, as well as a new FMC in Keat Hong.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: These will help to relieve the load in existing polyclinics in the West, such as Clementi Polyclinic.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will continue to review the regional primary care needs of our population and work closely with the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) and HDB to review and ensure the adequacy of the space needed for primary care facilities in HDB estates.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: A good primary care system can help to reduce costly interventions in the hospital setting.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To keep primary care affordable, CHAS and PG cardholders at the FMCs and CHAS clinics receive Government subsidies for their care.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng and Assoc Prof Daniel Goh commented on enhancing subsidies for primary care.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Since 2012, we have significantly enhanced CHAS so that more Singaporeans can benefit.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In 2013, we raised the income criterion from per capita monthly household income of $1,500 to $1,800.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In 2014, the age floor of 40 years was also removed.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: These changes have helped more Singaporean households to benefit from CHAS.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Assoc Prof Goh suggested that we change the per capita household income criterion of $1,800 to an individual's prevailing median monthly income of $3,900.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The current CHAS income criterion of $1,800 ensures that lower- to middle-income Singaporeans, or Singaporeans in about half of all resident households, can qualify.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This means that a household of four, with the breadwinner earning $7,200, is eligible.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: A household-based approach ensures that subsidies are equitably distributed to extend more benefits to individuals with more dependants.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In determining our income criterion, we will need to strike a balance, bearing in mind the need to target subsidies at those who need it most and Government budget availability.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will review CHAS regularly and enhance the scheme where needed to ensure that care remains affordable.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu asked for measures to improve transparency in the charging of healthcare services.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We have implemented various measures to this end.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Hospitals are required to provide financial counselling to patients to ensure that they are informed of the charges likely to be incurred for their treatment.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For outpatient care, patients are also provided with information on estimated charges for consultation.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Since 2013, hospital bill sizes for common conditions and procedures at both public and private hospitals have been progressively published on the MOH website.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: There will be further breakdown of the "Total Operation Fees" into "Surgeon Fees", "Anaesthetist Fees" as well as "Facility Fees".

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The expanded publication will provide added transparency on the private hospital bill components attributed to performing the procedure and serve as a point of reference for both healthcare professionals and the general public.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Safeguarding public health is another fundamental aspect of maintaining population health.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Even as we tackle the increasing prevalence of chronic diseases, we need to remain cognisant of our external environment.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In line with the Minister's call for us to remain vigilant, we need to constantly improve our public health system to promote health, prevent diseases and prolong life among our population.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We perform local and global surveillance to ensure situational awareness for endemic diseases, such as tuberculosis and influenza, and emerging diseases overseas, such as MERS and Zika.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We also fund research to evaluate the effectiveness of surveillance and response plans to infectious diseases.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: These include looking at potential areas for collaboration with the relevant institutions on Zika virus diagnostics, transmission and its association with microcephaly and Guillain-Barre Syndrome.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We conduct regular preparedness exercises to practise our responses and identify potential areas for improvements.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We also maintain a surge capacity for isolation beds and a national stockpile of personal protective equipment.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: While all GPs play important roles to provide care in such situations, PHPCs take on additional roles, such as providing subsidised care for conditions related to the public health emergencies.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Coordinated efforts across multiple Government agencies, as well as with other countries and international organisations, are also vital in protecting Singapore against external public health threats.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Nonetheless, there is currently no vaccine that confers 100% protection against all known strains of the dengue virus.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: If it is found to be efficacious locally and subsequently introduced, dengue vaccination should be coupled with other dengue control and healthcare strategies in Singapore, such as having a strong disease surveillance system and maintaining effective vector control measures, to keep the mosquito population low.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: All of us still have a part to play in staying alert and fighting dengue.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Let us encourage one another, including our children and youths, to adopt a healthy and active lifestyle to keep chronic diseases at bay.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Our regular family doctor shall be our trusted health partner throughout the different stages of our lives.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: At the same time, we introduce further measures for greater fee transparency at the hospitals.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Not forgetting our vulnerabilities in an increasingly connected global community, we will remain vigilant in responding to public health emergencies.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: On this note, I urge Singaporeans to partner us in building strong foundations for better care and better health.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: The threat of severe obesity noted in this paper was considered too severe to be tackled with medications or by exercise alone.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: The study recommended taxing foods that are high in sugar or that are highly processed.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: WHO has also recently come out in support of such a move.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: The level of obesity, as we have just heard, is also rising in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Obesity increases the risk of diabetes, heart disease, stroke, joint problems, high blood pressure, high cholesterol and certain types of cancer.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Not only does obesity have a negative impact on personal well-being; it is costly to the nation.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: We have to spend more money on obesity-related healthcare.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Other nations have imposed taxes on sugared beverages and on food which is high in saturated fats.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: I understand that such general taxes will raise prices and may disproportionality affect Singaporeans with lower incomes who spend a greater part of their income on food.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Unfortunately, unhealthy, processed food is often cheaper and more affordable.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: But just as taxes on alcohol and tobacco have nudged people into reducing their consumption, taxes on unhealthy food should be effective as well.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Sugar is arguably as significant a threat to public health as alcohol or tobacco, if not more.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: My rudimentary understanding of military strategy informs me that a key to winning a battle is to cut off the supply lines to the enemy and as we have just declared war on diabetes, I think such a move is tantamount to cutting the supply lines to the enemy, which is diabetes.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: By making healthier food cheaper than unhealthy food, hopefully, our people would start to change their eating habits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Singapore, like the UK, is experiencing an ageing population and the prevalence of obesity and heart disease.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: There are also local characteristics to the problem as Asians are at a higher risk of developing Type 2 diabetes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: It will, therefore, appear that we should seriously consider a sugar tax.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: However, the effectiveness of the sugar tax is questionable, at least in Singapore, as it will likely turn out to be a requisite tax on vulnerable Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The sugar content should also be colour-coded with green, amber and red.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Labelling should be in line with WHO guidelines of cutting free-sugar consumption to less than 10% of daily calorie intake.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: This can be rolled out in phases, starting with canned and packet drinks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: For example, a can of Coca Cola contains added sugar amounting to 80% of the current WHO guidelines and should be labelled red.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Health warnings that read "Drinking beverages with excessive added sugar contributes to obesity, diabetes and tooth decay" should be attached to drinks that are labelled red.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Studies to track whether labelling has resulted in consumers making better choices should be conducted to improve the labelling and gauge its success before we even consider a sugar tax.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: ElderShield is a severe disability insurance scheme with the purpose of providing basic financial protection to those who need long-term care, especially during old age.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: This is the 10th time I am speaking on ElderShield in this Chamber since 2002.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: I hope MOH will review ElderShield and make it more relevant towards addressing the long-term care of the severely disabled.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: These activities are washing, dressing, feeding, toileting, mobility and transferring.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: It is obvious that such patients are totally dependent on others for their daily living.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Therefore, how will $300 to $400 be enough to care for such patients in one month?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Even having a domestic helper to assist them will cost more than double in one month.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: I am concerned for those patients, especially the elderly, who do not have savings or  family members who can afford their dependent-care costs.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Some families take the option of sending their dependent members to hospitals or overstaying in acute hospitals even when they do not require to be hospitalised anymore.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Their actions not only deprive other patients who need hospital care, but they also incur tremendously high hospital costs.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: The patients may not feel the burden of the higher costs in acute hospitals, but it is to be noted that the bills are usually being paid by MediShield or MediFund for needy patients.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: The tenure of ElderShield payouts of a maximum of five to six years is also not adequate.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: These patients with three ADLs, especially those as a result of old age, are unlikely to get back to normal since they have reached the stage of inability to perform the daily activities.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Even for other sick patients with severe disabilities due to illnesses, such as stroke or cancer, reaching the stage of inability to perform daily activities, it will usually mean that their illnesses are too severe for them to regain normal activities again.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Thus, the insurance coverage of five to six years will leave them in a lurch at the end when their conditions could have deteriorated and should they require even more dependent-care at higher costs.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: These are the groups who are more likely to get severe disability.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: They are badly in need of ElderShield but are not eligible for this insurance.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: These are unaffordable premium amounts for many seniors and, therefore, many seniors are not in the scheme.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: One of the main reasons for people to take insurance is for peace of mind, knowing that finance is available should eventuality strike.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Thus, I hope MOH will review ElderShield to give better protection and assurance to the insured.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: MediShield Life had been revamped to give that assurance with its many improved features.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Maybe, now, MOH will consider revamping ElderShield to ElderShield Life, similarly as MediShield was improved to MediShield Life.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: The many new features of MediShield Life had been well thought out and they are very good.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Will MOH consider adopting these good features for ElderShield Life as well?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Lifelong coverage like MediShield Life is essential to give people the reassurance of coverage when they need the insurance most.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Patients usually reach their inability to perform ADL towards the end of their lives.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Therefore, it is good not to have the age limit on claims.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: The risk pool feature of MediShield should be adopted for ElderShield to make ElderShield more viable with non-opt out and as a comprehensive national scheme.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: I hope our Government will also give subsidies to those who cannot afford the premiums.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Presently, ElderShield is being administered by three private insurers.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: It will be better if CPF board takes over the role as in MediShield Life.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While MediShield Life is a good measure to cover all Singaporeans, it does not help with their living expenses when they are in recovery or out of the hospital.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, there are some improvements that I would like to suggest.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The premium costs are high for the lower-income families and the process to file claims may be overly burdensome, especially for the elderly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Does the Ministry have plans to review the premiums and also simplify the claim process?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Ministry also tap on the PG Office (PGO) to reach out to the other 35% of the resident population who are currently not covered by ElderShield?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, while the payout period has been extended to 72 months, will the Ministry consider extending the payout period for ElderShield to end of life instead, since there is no reason to assume that care needs would decrease after 72 months?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Sometimes, it can be almost like opening a different web browser app to view each different website.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: We should look at ways to enhance the use and user-friendliness of information technology (IT) in healthcare to improve productivity and patient safety everywhere.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We must also focus on developing a sustainable healthcare system.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: If we shift too far to the right, we will not be doing right by our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: If we overspend and shift too far to the left, our children will have nothing left in the future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Today, I shall talk about three areas to develop a sustainable healthcare system.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Second, transforming our care models by bringing care beyond hospitals into the community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Third, enhancing value through innovation and productivity improvements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To fight diabetes, we need a supportive environment to encourage Singaporeans to eat healthily and exercise regularly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Under the Healthy Living Master Plan, we introduced healthier dining options and provided more exercise options in the community, workplaces and schools.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: One such initiative is the Healthy Community Ecosystem, which has been implemented in six neighbourhoods since 2014, including my own Group Representation Constituency (GRC) in Bishan-Toa Payoh.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Group exercises are held in 40 community spaces, with an average of 1,000 residents participating each week.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Lifestyle modification programmes have reached 14,000 residents in these neighbourhoods.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Excessive consumption of sugar and refined carbohydrates can lead to weight gain and cause spikes in blood sugar levels.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Such spikes increase the risk of developing Type 2 diabetes, if they happen frequently over time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu asked about measures to discourage consumption of unhealthy food products.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh asked if we could introduce colour-coded labels for sugar content in processed food and drinks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will study their proposals as part of the fight against diabetes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Many food manufacturers already practise back-of-pack nutritional labelling.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: HPB's Healthier Choice Symbol (HCS) helps consumers make healthier purchases, through an identifiable front-of-pack symbol.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There are currently 2,500 HCS products across 70 food categories.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These products contain less sugar, saturated fat or salt.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: A 2015 consumer survey showed a high level of awareness of HCS products.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Nine in 10 said they recognised these products as healthier options and eight in 10 said they use HCS to guide their food purchases.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: HPB has worked with close to 240 supermarkets on in-store promotions, such as lucky draws, food sampling and cooking demonstrations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I am glad to know that HCS products are gaining market share.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Sales of HCS products are growing at 9% annually.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Some Members are concerned that healthier food may be more expensive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We need to work together with industry partners to provide affordable healthy options for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As of March this year, we have 52 food and beverage partners participating in the Healthier Dining Programme involving nearly 1,600 food stalls.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Under the programme, we collaborated with restaurants to offer lower calorie meal options and to incorporate healthier ingredients, such as whole grains, fruits and vegetables, as part of their core menu offerings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Major food court chains, including Kopitiam, Koufu and NTUC Foodfare, offer at least one dish below 500 calories at each stall.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I am encouraged by the industry's efforts to produce versions of staple foods, like bread and noodles, which are healthier and taste just as good.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Gardenia, for example, uses finely textured wholemeal flour to retain the health benefits of whole grains, while keeping its bread soft and easy to chew.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Besides eating right, we need to encourage Singaporeans to exercise regularly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The recommendation is to have at least 150 minutes of physical activity per week.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These 150 minutes can be achieved through simple daily activities like walking to the bus stop, using the stairs instead of the lift, doing household chores or taking a brisk walk at the park.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In 2013, one in four Singaporeans between the ages of 18 and 69 did not meet the 150 minutes per week target, and this was an increase from one in five in 2007.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Leading an active lifestyle can be simple and inexpensive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is also something we can enjoy with our family and friends.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: She is a regular participant at our Sundays at the Park programme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Every Sunday morning, she joins others in workout classes at the Firefly Park near her home in Clementi.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We hope to encourage more Singaporeans, including our seniors, to adopt active lifestyles like Mdm Jee.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Through the use of wearable technology and simple data analytics, users can receive feedback on their daily progress and also receive rewards when they reach certain milestones.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The National Steps Challenge has been well-received since its launch in November 2015.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: One in three participants have clocked 10,000 steps a day on average.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In addition, 70% of previously inactive participants now average more than 7,000 steps per day.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is a good start, as studies have shown that walking at least 7,500 steps a day can contribute to lower blood pressure and cholesterol levels and help those with diabetes keep their blood sugar levels in check.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Mohd Aidil Bin Sufyan found the Steps Tracker easy to use and a good way to motivate him to stay healthy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: He now takes the stairs more often and alights one bus stop earlier to walk home.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: He also brings his children for weekend walks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Apart from eating right and exercising more, it is important for Singaporeans to go for evidence-based health screening at recommended intervals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Early detection and treatment are important in the fight against diabetes, to keep the disease under control and prevent serious complications.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Individuals with diabetes can benefit from lifestyle changes to prevent their condition from worsening.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In addition, pre-diabetics could lower their risk of getting diabetes if they detect the problem early and improve their diet and lifestyle.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We plan to reach out to certain groups of Singaporeans below 40.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For example, those who are obese and those whose immediate family members have diabetes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They face a higher risk of getting diabetes and may need to start the screening at an earlier age.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will extend our screening outreach at the workplaces to bring diabetes screening to more workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These include those who may find it difficult to schedule screening appointments due to the nature of their jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will also review ways to strengthen post-screening follow-up to initiate early treatment and care when needed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Next, I will touch on efforts to move care beyond hospitals into the community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MOH has co-located several community hospitals with acute hospitals to facilitate care integration for patients.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are helping patients to shorten their stays at community hospitals and return home earlier.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For example, by allowing them to do their rehabilitation follow-ups at day rehabilitation centres.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is what many of our patients prefer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They do not want to stay in the hospitals longer than necessary.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As our population ages, it is inevitable that some of us will become frail and disabled and require support in activities of daily living.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For some, this may be a few years before they pass on.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For others, the duration could be longer, as Dr Lily Neo and Mr Louis Ng highlighted.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There were also earlier proposals from the People's Action Party (PAP) Seniors Group.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, this higher cost will, ultimately, be borne by everyone, whether directly through ElderShield premiums or indirectly through tax-funded subsidies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Hence, there is a need to balance enhancements in ElderShield with the potential cost increases, so that the scheme can remain affordable for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: ElderShield payout is one important source of payment but it is not the only source.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Pioneers, for example, can receive Pioneer Generation Disability Assistance Scheme (PioneerDAS) on top of ElderShield.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, we will look at different ways of helping our seniors, especially those who are disabled.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is now an opt-out scheme, as some Members have pointed out, and how do we provide coverage for older cohorts of Singaporeans who, today, may not have ElderShield?

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Similar to how we enhanced MediShield into MediShield Life, MOH will need to carefully review ElderShield in consultation with experts and key stakeholders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our end in mind is to provide Singaporeans with peace of mind when we grow old, while keeping the scheme affordable for all.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MOH is working in partnership with the palliative care sector under the National Strategy for Palliative Care.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Since 2014, we have ramped up capacity and improved the quality of palliative care in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Dr Lily Neo asked for better provision of hospice care, including training of hospice care personnel.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have introduced guidelines for the palliative care sector and will work with the Singapore Hospice Council to encourage industry players to adopt these guidelines.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Dr Lily Neo and Mr Low Thia Khiang asked about the financing framework for hospices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MOH regularly reviews funding for the palliative care sector to ensure end-of-life remains affordable for patients and sustainable for providers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In July 2012, we raised the threshold for per capita household monthly income to cover up to two-thirds of Singaporean households, up from half previously.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This has benefited more than 1,000 additional patients.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will continue to review and adjust the income threshold, like what we have done before.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have also enhanced financial support for hospice care services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In 2014, we improved funding for home palliative care providers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Last year, we increased the MediSave withdrawal limit for inpatient hospice and home palliative care.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Just last month, we increased subsidies for eligible inpatient hospice patients and introduced subsidies for day hospice care.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Overall, with coverage from Government subsidies, charity assistance and MediSave, most patients do not face out-of-pocket payments for hospice and palliative care.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For inpatient hospice, the median length of stay is 15 days.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Last year, MOH received three appeals on hospice care costs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I agree with Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin that it is important for end-of-life care to be provided with empathy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We do have training for our healthcare professionals in this area and will look at ways to further improve and do better.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In addition, MOH is supportive of other efforts to improve the quality of our end-of-life care, for example, Assisi Hospice's new facility, where the design of wards resembles a home rather than an institution.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Outdoor gardens and green spaces are also included as part of the development.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: VWOs play an invaluable role in the end-of-life care sector to provide quality and affordable care.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We want to preserve this strong community support and involvement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Programmes by volunteers also help patients to live their last days fully.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This includes befriending and psycho-social support for patients and their families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will support innovations in palliative care and will continue to work with providers, like Assisi Hospice and others, to pilot new ideas that can benefit patients and caregivers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Tan asked whether existing private patients in SOCs are allowed to switch to subsidised care without a polyclinic referral.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: If a private SOC patient wants to switch to subsidised care, a medical social worker will assess his request.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These assessments are done on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is to ensure that we target our subsidies at patients with the greatest financial need.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For new patients seeking subsidised specialist care, they will first go through a primary care doctor to assess if they need specialist care services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This can be done at a polyclinic or CHAS GP clinic, if he is a CHAS or PG card holder.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We know there are some private SOC patients who choose to be discharged from private SOC and go through this route to switch to subsidised SOC, instead of going through a medical social worker at the hospital.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Strictly speaking, this is not part of the policy for patients to downgrade from private to subsidised SOC.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is perhaps why Mr Tan pointed out that the arrangement is not very neat and tidy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: However, our hospitals want to be flexible and they have accommodated these private patients, so that they are not treated differently from new patients who go through the polyclinic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Taking a broader view, our priority is to transform the way we care for patients, by bringing it beyond the hospital into the community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I shared about how we are integrating care between acute and community hospitals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In addition, MOH is piloting new models where specialists work closely with polyclinics and GPs to co-manage patients who have chronic conditions and need ongoing care.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are also building up primary care so that more SOC patients who are stable can be discharged and cared for by the polyclinics or GPs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is a more impactful and sustainable way to have a win-win arrangement for everyone.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked about Integrated Shield Plans, or IPs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These are private insurance plans which work together with MediShield Life.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MOH sets the premiums for the MediShield Life component and we will keep MediShield Life premiums affordable for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The private insurance premiums are decided by insurers based on commercial and actuarial considerations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They will review and adjust these premiums based on factors, such as claims experience.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: If claims were to increase significantly over time, the insurers will likely increase their premiums, as some have recently done so with the premiums for riders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Singaporeans who want to keep their insurance premiums affordable, including at older ages when premiums tend to go up, should carefully consider if you want to purchase private insurance like IPs and riders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Some of my residents in Bishan-Toa Payoh told me that they think MediShield Life is adequate to provide them with good quality subsidised care.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I agree with Mr Pritam Singh that it is important to guard against over-consumption and over-charging.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These will exert upward pressure on healthcare costs and insurance premiums over time, a concern that was shared by Dr Chia Shi-Lu.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is why MediShield Life and all IPs have co-payment features.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will work with insurers to review existing features in private insurance schemes to mitigate the risk of over-consumption and over-charging, while providing sufficient coverage and peace of mind for policyholders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Other important initiatives to keep healthcare costs and premiums affordable include: promoting healthy living and active ageing because we know prevention is better than cure; finding ways to improve productivity in the healthcare sector; encouraging appropriate care to reduce over-treatment or over-prescription; and, providing more information on fees and charges to help patients decide which hospital and doctor they want to visit.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MOH will work closely with our healthcare institutions and the Healthcare Services Employees' Union to encourage and support ideas that can enhance patient care and service quality, improve the work environment for our healthcare workers and make our healthcare system more productive and sustainable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng asked about enhancing the use of information technology, particularly in the sharing of medical records.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I agree with Dr Tan that this will help to improve productivity and patient care.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We rolled out NEHR in 2012 for participating healthcare institutions to view their patients' events and summary health records.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As at March 2016, there are more than 900 healthcare institutions with access to NEHR and we would like to include more healthcare institutions over time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Technology is a key enabler to improve the work environment for healthcare workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: When I visited NUH, I saw their pilot project to remotely monitor patients' vital signs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: With this system, the time nurses spend monitoring patients' vital signs has reduced by half.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I am also very happy to know that there are other areas where we can support such technology, including a chair that I saw.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It looks like a normal chair but when you use it, and if you press a button, it will automatically wrap and seal the waste products.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, this makes it easier for the nurses and caregivers, as there is no unpleasant smell and the waste disposal can be done more conveniently.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Ms Thanaletchimi asked about the training for healthcare workers as we implement automation and robotics.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The public healthcare employers are committed to redesigning jobs and supporting our workers to gain new skills so that they can stay employable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In fact, through technology and productivity improvements, we want to enable healthcare workers to remain longer in service by making the work less physically demanding for them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is a win-win arrangement – workers can continue working for more years, while patients can benefit from their service and experience.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They partnered the AIC to do a job redesign and, through the various changes they have made, the staff were able to save up to 20% of their time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They also introduced FWAs so as to allow staff more flexibility in managing their work hours.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our healthcare workers play a pivotal role in supporting productivity initiatives and we appreciate and recognise their efforts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Ms Thanaletchimi suggested extending the Progressive Wage Model which we currently have in the healthcare system to other groups of healthcare workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MOH will work with the union on this.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We want to retain our healthcare workers and upskill them to provide quality care for our patients.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is reflected in the improvements in our life expectancy and health outcomes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Credit must go to our committed healthcare workers, who have put in a lot of dedication and hard work to care for their patients.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We must continue to show appreciation for their efforts, support them in their work and also stand by our healthcare workers during difficult times.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For future generations of Singaporeans to continue having affordable, accessible and quality healthcare, we need to transform our care models and keep our healthcare system sustainable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To succeed, it will require the involvement of all Singaporeans − from individuals, families and the community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It will require changes in habits and behaviours.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And, most importantly, it will require all stakeholders to work together in close collaboration and partnership.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We have a bit of time for clarifications.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: As I understand it, it now regulates medical devices and cosmetic products and I also understand there have been some public consultations on this about whether it is possible to transfer the control of other pharmaceutical products under this Act.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Could I ask the Minister for an update on the status of this transfer and whether it is likely that we will see an amendment to the Act in the near future?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: The second clarification concerns this threat of infectious diseases, and it is directed to Minister of State Dr Lam Pin Min.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: In view of the potential cost of an epidemic, should it occur, do we have provision for a fund to deal with the cost of tackling the epidemic and also the resultant economic cost?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: If we look at the US, for instance, they set up a fund to combat Ebola.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Now that the threat has passed, they are porting some money over to combat the threat of Zika and  expanding on that fund.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: So, I am just wondering whether we have a provision for a fund to tackle such public health crises.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: The final clarification is with regard to my cut on transparency.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Dr Chia, can you keep your clarification short.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Could I just ask if there are any more concrete steps that we can take to, perhaps modulate the cost of private healthcare?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Dr Chia is right that we are looking at health product regulations and looking at the pharmaceutical products that are currently regulated under the Medicines Act.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is in line with our plan to update our legislation and to consolidate the regulation of health-related products in one Act for greater clarity.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We held two rounds of public consultation recently.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Sorry, Mdm Chair, can I answer the other two questions asked by Dr Chia Shi-Lu?

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In addition to that, like I have mentioned in my reply, we do stockpile medical equipment and supplies like our personal protective equipment, anti-microbials and even vaccines, if necessary.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: With regard to the second clarification on the control of costs in the private sector, in my speech, I did mention that we have published the professional fees on our MOH website which include total hospitalisation fees both in the public and private sector, the total operation fees in the public sector.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: And most recently, like I have just announced, we will be publishing the total operation fees of the private hospitals, and this will actually serve as a point of reference for both the healthcare professionals as well as the general public, so that they can make an informed decision.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Minister Gan Kim Yong has also announced the setting up of ACE, and this agency will evaluate the clinical and cost effectiveness of health technologies and all the different expensive treatment modalities.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Thirdly, our healthcare insurance financing features like co-payment and deductibles are built into our MediShield Life as well as some private healthcare plans and this will, hopefully, discourage the "buffet syndrome".

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Last but not least, which is the most important, is that I would like to remind all doctors that we are bound by the Singapore Medical Council and Singapore Dental Council's ethical code and ethical guidelines and that we should not abuse the doctor-patient relationship for our own personal gains.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: From the patients' point of view, whether the data is meaningful or not, is something we need to consider.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: From the patients' point of view, what we do for SOC services is to prioritise their needs and fix their schedule according to the seriousness of their conditions.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For those who have more serious and time-sensitive conditions, we will give them priority.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The published wait time may not mean a lot to them and may create more confusion, because some of them may have to wait longer than the median wait time because their conditions are less critical, and some may have earlier appointments because of their serious conditions.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: From the patients' point of view, we have to be careful with the data we publish.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But we do monitor the wait times at our SOCs for our hospitals.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Whether they are published or not, it is a performance indicator that we keep track of.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: The first one, just now, Senior Minister of State Amy Khor had mentioned and provided some explanation about the community networks for seniors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: At the same time, I am just wondering if the Ministry will also consider establishing something like an eldercare relationship management system so that there is a more systematic way for the different stakeholders to integrate our efforts and to synchronise in how we can reach and better care for our elderly.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Second, I would like to ask whether there is any plan to leverage more on technology to enable ageing-in-place so that our elders in their retirement can live in a more independent manner.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: The third query is on the Trim and Fit (TAF) programme.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: I understand that, in the past, in the schools, there is the TAF programme to encourage the young to be healthier.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: So, just wondering why this has been discontinued and what is the reason for that.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Lastly, on Zika, just yesterday, there was news from the US that it is worse than it has been previously thought.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: It affects the entire pregnancy period and so this is quite worrying.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Also, I fear that awareness about Zika in Singapore is still very much lagging, especially compared to dengue.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Tin, can you keep it trim and fit, please?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: So, may I ask the Ministry what is it going to do to increase awareness towards Zika?

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will try and look at what the gaps are and so on.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With regard to the Member's suggestion about getting grassroots involved, indeed, community networks will involve all stakeholders in the community.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It is just that it will be facilitated by a small team of staff together with the various Government agencies, the VWOs, community-based organisations and, of course, including grassroots.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Because we are piloting the project, we will certainly take into account the Member's strong interest in setting up a community network.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Let us pilot it and learn from it before we can scale up.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Regarding eldercare relationships, in fact, this is what we have been doing under the Action Plan for Successful Ageing.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: After learning from implementing the many ground-up ideas, we have put it into a guide and sent it to all the divisions.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: When we learn through the community networks, we can also put up some of these as guiding principles for use.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: That is why I have said in my speech earlier that there is a National Innovation Challenge where we have made two grant calls and we will be calling for more.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The first two are on new models of home-care and enhancing care for dementia.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Along with these, we will be looking at technology, too.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In fact, there are some pilots, with regard to technology, say in Marine Parade, where they are piloting a home-monitoring system to monitor the health as well as the lives of the elderly to make sure they are taken care of.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: If something happens, they can actually alert the senior care centres.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Ms Tin is probably young enough to have either personally experienced the TAF programme or have witnessed her classmates going through it.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It addresses other aspects of physical health as well as mental and social health.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: So, that is the reason and the answer to the Member's first clarification.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: One, to reduce the risk of importation; two, early detection; and three, containment.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In reducing the risk of importation, MOH issues travel advisories on affected countries for Singaporeans who are travelling out of Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Even for women who may get pregnant, they are advised strongly not to travel to these affected countries unless there is a strong reason to do so.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To enhance early detection, we have enhanced vigilance amongst our healthcare providers as well as public healthcare institutions.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We also have to step up public education amongst the general public about this disease.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: If we do have a first case of positive Zika infection, then isolation will be necessary to prevent its spread through the bites on this infected person by the Aedes mosquito.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: But, of course, not forgetting the good old effective vector control.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I think all of us have a part to play in performing the 5-step Mozzie Wipeout routine.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To manage pregnant patients who may be affected by Zika, MOH has also set up a clinical advisory group on Zika virus infection and pregnancy and it comprises obstetricians, public health specialists as well as infectious disease specialists who advise MOH on the different aspects of management of  a pregnant patient who may be suspected of being infected with Zika.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: So, I want to reassure Ms Tin Pei Ling that MOH will closely monitor the development of Zika infection overseas as well as the development of other potential treatment modalities including vaccines.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Keep it short, please, since you have four questions.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: On healthy living and preventive health, could I check with the Minister if there are any plans to roll out the holistic electronic health record of a Singaporean from birth to school, work and through retirement in a holistic way?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: The second clarification is on promoting healthy eating habits.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: How can we help low-wage and vulnerable workers eat healthily, to have better healthy options for choice, if the cost of healthy choice options is rather high at workplaces or in industry sectors?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: The third clarification is whether the Minister would consider reviewing the MediSave withdrawal limit, especially on flexi-MediSave capped at $200, so that those affected patients who are seeking specialist treatment can better manage their chronic disease or illness.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: Lastly, would MOH revive or further explore the possibility of a portable medical benefits scheme which employers can offer workers in the early stage of employment so that workers can carry with them the medical benefit plan even if they were to be retrenched or lose their jobs?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I am very supportive of these portable medical benefits and I think it is a great thing.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The most portable medical benefit is really MediShield Life.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I would encourage employers to think about helping their employees with their MediShield Life, either by topping up their MediSave so that they can use their MediSave top-up to pay for the MediShield Life premiums, or purchase IPs for their employees.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I will now ask my colleague, Minister of State Chee Hong Tat, to talk about MediSave withdrawal limits that the Member has asked about, as well as healthy eating habits, how to help the low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, I would encourage you to download this app which you can carry in your handphone and it is available to you 24/7 all the time.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It is something that we are working on and we will continue to enhance this app.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is just a pilot application and it is still at the beta stage.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We encourage you to download it, use it and let us have your feedback on how it is working and we will continue to enhance its features to make it useful for individuals.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We want to use this to empower our individuals to lead a healthy lifestyle.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Indeed, we have to find ways to make healthier food options affordable.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In some of the institutions and companies, in their cafeteria or canteen, they do offer healthier options.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: When I visited Khoo Teck Puat Hospital, they were showing me the food court.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If you eat brown rice, it is cheaper than if you eat white rice.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It Is not the case in all places, but at the food court in Khoo Teck Puat Hospital, that is the pricing incentive that they give to encourage people to eat healthily.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: They also give a discount if you order drinks with less sugar.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If you order kopi-C, it is more expensive than if you order kopi-C xiu dai, and it is more expensive than if you order kopi-C kosong.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, they try to find different ways to nudge people to eat healthily.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: They also use design to try and place the different food items.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is also about how you encourage good behaviours, eating habits.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The economic rice stall, for example, they will put the healthier options at the beginning of the queue, so that when you choose these options, by the end of the queue where some of the less healthy foods are, your plate would be full and, therefore, you may not have as much incentive, desire or temptation to order the less healthy food.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Through this combination of ways, they are trying to help the visitors, patrons and also their own staff to eat more healthily.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We also need the help of the unions and our Labour Movement to help us to work together to try and encourage all Singaporeans, including our workers, to eat healthily.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In 2014, when we looked at the amount, it was sufficient for the majority of patients.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For eight in 10 patients, this amount was sufficient.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But in certain cases where the need may be greater, they can actually share with their spouse.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, it is not just your own individual account.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: You can use it to help your spouse.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This also gives greater flexibility in cases where they need a little bit more.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Very importantly, while we look at ways to provide more flexibility through the use of MediSave, we must also bear in mind that MediSave, at the end, is also used for long-term healthcare needs when we grow old.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is used to pay for our healthcare costs and to pay for our insurance premiums, including MediShield Life premiums.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, there is a need to strike a balance.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But we will look at ways to try and make it flexible for people to use and to keep the cost affordable for chronic disease management.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: One, for the Minister, is whether the Ministry will consider the suggestion I made to publish the waiting times separately for walk-in versus appointment for polyclinics, and to lower the key performance indicator from 100 minutes to 45 minutes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: My second clarification point is to Minister of State Chee Hong Tat regarding the outreach efforts to companies through health talks and healthy living promotion.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: One of the best ways to reach out to adults is through their employers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I know HPB does programmes, such as screening and talks, with large employers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: What more will HPB be doing to reach out to SMEs to conduct this kind of programmes, perhaps working together with the trade associations and chambers?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In saying that, I should also clarify that in the primary sector, such as polyclinics that the Member was referring to, we have more critical issues at hand because we are in the process of restructuring the whole primary care sector, as Dr Lam has outlined.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Over time, we should look at primary care not just between polyclinics and GPs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are in the process of restructuring and revamping the primary care sector.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Our indicators and performance targets have to be in line with the new model that we are evolving.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will take on board the Member's suggestion and study very carefully but, at the same time, bear in mind that the sector is going through a transformation.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is not just between polyclinic and GPs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are also trying to integrate SOCs with primary care, so that we minimise the need to refer cases to the SOCs and to also facilitate discharge of SOC patients to primary care, so that they can be taken care of in a primary care setting.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In orthopaedics today − I think Dr Chia Shi-Lu would be very familiar with − primary care and polyclinic patients cannot have direct access to physiotherapy without being referred to orthopaedic specialists because we are concerned about the missed-diagnosis.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But we have developed protocols to facilitate primary care doctors to make a preliminary diagnosis and, in many cases, you do not require the services of a specialist and you can refer patients directly to a physiotherapist.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We want to try it out to see whether this works well for us.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: If it does, we will encourage more in the primary sector to take on this responsibility.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In doing so, you will find that between GPs and polyclinic, between primary care and specialist care, it is going to be more and more integrated.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The indicators that we use will also have to take that into account.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: How do we measure the outcome, not in a segmented way, each individual department's or setting's performance, but an integrated performance measurement?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It is something that is evolving, and we will consider the Member's suggestions and incorporate some of them.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: My clarification is on the expansion of healthcare demand which the Minister spoke about earlier.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Are there sufficient resources given to this area?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: For long-term benefits and future needs, will the Minister not curtail, for whatever reasons, the specialist training of local doctors?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But we do also want to ensure that there are sufficient numbers of local doctors that go into family medicine because family medicine is going to play an increasingly important role.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As I explained just now, family medicine will play a very important role in our review of primary care.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Therefore, we want to encourage our doctors to pursue further education, both in specialist as well as family medicine training.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Having said that, despite the expansion in the pipeline, expansion in our training capacity, we will still need to look at the need of supplementing our local manpower with foreign trained manpower.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The first part of foreign trained manpower is our own Singaporeans who are trained overseas.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have a lot of programmes to reach out to them, including our Pre-employment Grant (PEG), where we work with our students who are receiving training overseas to attract them back to Singapore to serve in our public sector.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Our greatest allies are the parents because the parents do want their children to return.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, we work with them to bring them back.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I have one parent who came to me to say, "Can you please give my son the PEG?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I will fund you, but make sure he signs the contract to come back." We do go out of our way to reach out to them, engage them, provide them with the opportunity to return.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In between their studies, if there are opportunities, we will also want to bring them back for internship, training and so on, so that they remain connected to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We hope to be able to do more of this, going forward.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: On behalf of Members, I would like to thank the tireless staff of MOH and, of course, Minister Gan, Senior Minister of State Amy Khor, Minister of State Lam Pin Min and Minister of State Chee Hong Tat for their meticulous replies and clarifications.

text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.05 pm.
